species.name: Tawny Owl
species.identification: A rounded woodland owl with dark eyes, a broad facial disc and mottled brown plumage. Its short tail and rounded wings give it a compact silhouette; there are no ear tufts.
species.habitat: Broadleaf and mixed woodland, including mature trees in parks and larger gardens.
species.range: Resident in England, Wales and Scotland, but absent from Ireland. Established pairs usually remain within the same territory.
species.diet: Mostly small mammals such as mice and voles, with birds, amphibians, large insects and earthworms also taken.
species.behaviour: Usually active after dark and concealed in a tree during daylight. Territorial calling becomes conspicuous as young birds disperse in autumn.
species.voice: The familiar owl duet combines a sharp contact call, usually from the female, with the male's wavering hoot.
species.breeding: Uses tree cavities or nest boxes. Incubation starts with the first egg, so chicks hatch at different times.
species.interestingFact: On wet nights, a Tawny Owl may hunt earthworms on a lawn as well as larger prey.

species.name: Goldcrest
species.identification: A tiny olive-green and grey bird with pale underparts, white wing bars and a large dark eye. Black borders frame its yellow crown; males also have orange in the crown's centre.
species.habitat: Coniferous and mixed woodland, plus parks and gardens with mature trees. Look among the outer needles and fine branches.
species.range: Widespread in the UK. Resident birds are joined in winter by migrants from Scandinavia and Russia.
species.diet: Small insects picked from foliage with a very fine, pointed bill.
species.behaviour: Keeps moving through the canopy and may hang upside down while searching for food. In winter it can travel with mixed flocks of tits.
species.voice: A thin, very high song repeats insistently, helping reveal a tiny bird hidden among conifer branches.
species.breeding: A female can lay as many as twelve eggs, a substantial reproductive investment for such a small bird.
species.interestingFact: Alongside the Firecrest, it is the UK's smallest bird. Despite weighing only about six grams, migrating Goldcrests make their journeys under their own power.

species.name: Carrion Crow
species.identification: Glossy black all over, with a sturdy black bill. Adults of both sexes and young birds look broadly alike. Its flight often has steady, unhurried wingbeats.
species.habitat: An adaptable bird of farmland, woodland, moorland, coasts, gardens and city streets.
species.range: Widespread across much of Britain. Hooded Crows largely replace it in northern and western Scotland and Ireland; the two can hybridise where their ranges meet.
species.diet: An opportunist taking carrion, seeds, fruit, scraps, eggs and young birds.
species.behaviour: Often seen alone or in pairs. It can be cautious around a new food source, returning once it has assessed the surroundings.
species.breeding: Builds a stick nest in a tree or on structures including buildings, cliffs and electricity pylons. Nesting birds can be surprisingly unobtrusive.
species.interestingFact: A flock is not automatically a group of Rooks: Carrion Crows sometimes join Rooks and Jackdaws in winter gatherings.

species.name: Herring Gull
species.identification: A large gull with a white head and body, grey back, pink feet and black wing tips marked with white. Adults have a yellow bill with a red spot; young birds are mottled brown.
species.habitat: Seashores and coastal cliffs, but also fields, lakes, reservoirs and urban rooftops.
species.range: Present around the UK throughout the year. Inland waters and farmland can be especially useful places to look in winter.
species.diet: Takes fish, insects, carrion and discarded food. It may patter its feet on the ground to bring worms to the surface.
species.behaviour: Parents defend the area around their nest and chicks. Pairs often remain together and return to a nesting site in later years.
species.breeding: Usually begins breeding at around four years old. Nests may be on the ground, a cliff ledge or a roof, with two or three eggs typical.
species.interestingFact: A chick pecks at the adult's red bill spot as a signal requesting food.

species.name: Peregrine
species.identification: A powerful falcon with pointed wings, a short tail and dark facial markings resembling a moustache. Adults are blue-grey above with barred pale underparts. Females are larger; juveniles are browner and streaked below.
species.habitat: Rocky coasts, crags and quarries, with tall city buildings also providing nesting places.
species.range: Breeds across suitable UK habitats, with strongholds in northern and western uplands. Some upland birds move towards lower ground, estuaries and coasts in winter.
species.diet: Mostly other birds, including pigeons and waders. Smaller birds and occasional bats are also taken.
species.behaviour: Pursues prey in flight and can attack in a steep, exceptionally fast dive. Its agility also matters during aerial chases.
species.breeding: Uses elevated ledges on cliffs and buildings; cathedrals can provide an urban counterpart to natural rocky nesting sites.
species.interestingFact: A partly transparent third eyelid protects its eyes during high-speed flight while allowing it to keep its target in view.

species.name: Merlin
species.identification: A small falcon with pointed wings and a short, square-ended tail. The male has a blue-grey back and rusty, streaked underparts; females and young birds are browner, with streaking on a pale underside.
species.habitat: Heather moorland in the breeding season, then often lowland farmland, saltmarsh and other open coastal habitats in winter.
species.range: Breeds mainly in northern and western UK uplands. Many birds move to lower ground for winter, when arrivals from Iceland add to the population.
species.diet: Hunts small birds, pursuing them with quick changes of direction in the air.
species.behaviour: Rapid wingbeats alternate with brief glides, with the wings held close to the body. Its compact shape helps distinguish it from the longer-tailed Kestrel.
species.breeding: Typically raises one brood, with four or five eggs. The female undertakes most incubation.
species.interestingFact: The UK's smallest bird of prey, a male Merlin is only a little larger than a Blackbird.

species.name: Rook
species.identification: An adult has bare pale skin around the base of its pointed bill, a peaked head and glossy black plumage. Loose feathers around the legs can suggest trousers. Young Rooks lack the adult's bare face.
species.habitat: Farmland, villages and towns with mature trees suitable for nesting and roosting.
species.range: A widespread UK bird of the countryside, also living in settlements where feeding areas and nesting trees are available.
species.diet: Eats insects and seeds, alongside small mammals, eggs and young birds.
species.behaviour: Feeds, nests and roosts socially. Winter roosts may include Jackdaws, with large groups departing together to feed.
species.voice: Communal roosts become noisy as birds gather at dusk or leave around dawn.
species.breeding: Nests in treetop colonies called rookeries. Birds repair nests with twigs from late winter, and a rookery may persist for decades.
species.interestingFact: Rooks can bury food for later and use their memory to find these hidden supplies again.

species.name: Robin
species.identification: Adults have an orange-red face and breast against a brown back. Males and females look alike. Young Robins are speckled golden-brown and initially lack the familiar red breast.
species.habitat: Gardens, parks and other wooded or shrubby places, from countryside to city neighbourhoods.
species.range: Widespread across the UK and visible throughout the year.
species.diet: Worms and insect grubs are among the foods it takes when freshly turned soil exposes them.
species.behaviour: May approach a working gardener closely, yet strongly defends its territory against other Robins.
species.voice: A flowing series of high whistles, trills and short phrases, often separated by pauses. Song can be heard through much of the year, becoming quieter during the summer moult.
species.breeding: Nests in sheltered nooks, including open-fronted boxes and flowerpots. Four or five eggs are usual, with several nesting attempts possible in a season.
species.interestingFact: Street lighting can prompt a Robin to sing after dark, making it a familiar night-time voice in towns.

species.name: Blackbird
species.identification: An adult male is black with a yellow-orange bill and yellow eye ring. Females and juveniles are brown, with markings on the breast rather than the male's uniform dark plumage.
species.habitat: Gardens, parks, woodland, hedgerows, farmland and coastal scrub, with ground cover for searching and places to perch.
species.range: Widespread around the UK, apart from the highest ground. Birds arriving from northern Europe increase winter numbers.
species.diet: Earthworms, caterpillars and other invertebrates are especially important during breeding. It also eats fleshy fruits, including hawthorn and ivy berries.
species.behaviour: Frequently feeds on the ground, hopping between patches and turning leaves over. Singing males choose exposed high perches such as treetops or roofs.
species.voice: Rich, mellow phrases are especially noticeable at dawn and dusk in spring and early summer. Alarm calls include sharp chucks and rattling bursts.
species.breeding: The female constructs a nest incorporating twigs and mud, usually laying three or four eggs. Further broods may follow in fresh nests.
species.interestingFact: A winter garden can host both local Blackbirds and visitors that have travelled from northern Europe.

species.name: Blue Tit
species.identification: A small tit with a blue cap, blue wings, yellow chest and greenish back. A black stripe crosses its white face through the eye; the bill is short and fine.
species.habitat: Woodland, hedges, parks and gardens, often making acrobatic visits to garden feeders.
species.range: Found through most of the UK, with gaps on some Scottish islands.
species.diet: Takes food including nuts at feeders, while caterpillars are especially important for growing chicks.
species.behaviour: Clings to branches and feeders while searching for food. In winter it often joins other tits in travelling flocks, keeping contact with calls.
species.voice: Its song combines high notes with a lower trill or rattling finish. Calls can be heard throughout the year.
species.breeding: The female builds the nest. Usually one large clutch is timed so that hungry chicks coincide with abundant caterpillars.
species.interestingFact: Blue Tits famously learned to open the foil tops of doorstep milk bottles to reach the cream beneath.

species.name: Great Tit
species.identification: The largest UK tit has a glossy black head, white cheeks and yellow underparts divided by a black stripe. Its back is greenish; the stripe down the breast is usually more substantial in males.
species.habitat: Deciduous woodland and scrub, but also parks and gardens where it readily uses feeders.
species.range: Widespread in Britain and Ireland, except for some islands in northern and western Scotland.
species.diet: Mainly insects in summer. Garden feeders provide additional food during winter.
species.behaviour: Can displace smaller tits at feeding stations. Outside the breeding season it often joins roaming mixed flocks searching trees and gardens.
species.voice: A repeated two-note phrase is a useful starting point for recognition, although the species has many other songs and calls.
species.breeding: Readily occupies nest boxes. Usually lays one clutch in a year, though a second is possible.
species.interestingFact: A familiar garden visitor still retains its woodland habits, travelling with other tit species in winter feeding parties.

species.name: Wren
species.identification: A tiny, rounded brown bird with a fine pointed bill, pale eyebrow and delicate barring on the darker wings. Its very short tail is often cocked upright. Both sexes look similar.
species.habitat: Dense vegetation in gardens, woods and farmland, as well as rocky crevices and sheltered banks.
species.range: Widespread across the UK, though severe, prolonged cold can greatly affect this small bird.
species.diet: Searches for insects, adding seeds and berries, particularly when insects are harder to find in winter.
species.behaviour: Moves quickly through cover and can be difficult to spot despite living close to people. It may emerge onto a higher perch to sing.
species.voice: An unexpectedly powerful song of high whistles ending in a trill, plus a sharp repeated ticking call.
species.breeding: The male builds several nests. A female chooses one, lines it with feathers and commonly lays five or six eggs.
species.interestingFact: Wrens sometimes crowd into nest boxes to share warmth during cold conditions.

species.name: Magpie
species.identification: Black and white plumage and a long, stiff tail make this crow relative distinctive. Good light reveals blue-purple reflections on the wings and a green sheen along the tail.
species.habitat: Towns, suburbs, villages and farmland. Its flexible habits allow it to live in landscapes shaped by people.
species.range: Widespread through much of Britain and Ireland, but scarce in northern and north-western Scotland and on many Scottish islands.
species.diet: A flexible feeder that scavenges and hunts; eggs and young birds are among its prey.
species.behaviour: Curious and conspicuous. Birds that are not breeding may gather in flocks.
species.voice: A harsh, rapidly repeated chatter is especially noticeable when a bird is agitated.
species.breeding: Usually raises one brood. A typical clutch contains five or six eggs, incubated by the female for about twenty days.
species.interestingFact: Its tail contributes at least a third of its total length, so much of the familiar silhouette is tail rather than body.

species.name: Woodpigeon
species.identification: A large grey pigeon with a pinkish breast, pale eye and conspicuous white neck patches. Broad white marks on the wings stand out when it takes flight.
species.habitat: Woodland, farmland, parks, grassland and garden lawns. It has adapted readily to towns and cities.
species.range: Resident through much of the UK, with winter numbers augmented by birds from continental Europe.
species.diet: Eats leaves, buds, berries and seeds, including beechmast. Green vegetation is important in winter; newly hatched chicks receive nutritious crop milk.
species.behaviour: Often wary in rural places but much more approachable in towns. Large flocks can pass overhead during autumn migration.
species.voice: Its mellow cooing is a familiar woodland sound. Take-off can also announce the bird with a sudden loud clatter of wings.
species.breeding: Can nest in any season when conditions permit, although summer is the main breeding period. A clutch usually contains two eggs.
species.interestingFact: The huge autumn movements seen over parts of Britain are still not fully understood; observers cannot assume that every flock shares the same origin or destination.

species.name: Chaffinch
species.identification: Males combine pink and chestnut tones with blue-grey plumage. Females and juveniles are quieter yellow-brown. White wing markings and pale outer tail feathers can be striking when either sex flies.
species.habitat: Woodland and gardens, with hedges and seed-rich farmland also used for feeding.
species.range: Present across much of Britain and Ireland all year. Winter brings additional birds from northern Europe, including Fennoscandia.
species.diet: Seeds provide an important feeding opportunity, including in farmland strips planted to support wild birds.
species.behaviour: Often hops below feeders or hedges to search the ground. It may form mixed winter flocks with other finches.
species.voice: A strong song runs down the scale and finishes with a flourish. A varied set of calls can reveal a bird concealed nearby.
species.breeding: A typical clutch contains four or five eggs. The distinctive song becomes especially evident during the breeding season.
species.interestingFact: Its patterned plumage can conceal a ground-feeding Chaffinch until the white wing and tail markings flash in flight.

species.name: Starling
species.identification: Smaller than a Blackbird, with a short tail and pointed wings. Dark plumage gleams purple and green nearby; pale spotting is especially obvious in winter. The bill changes from dark in winter to yellow in summer.
species.habitat: Gardens and other open feeding places. Large communal roosts can form in reedbeds, on piers and around coastal marshes.
species.range: Resident across much of the UK, with gaps in parts of Scotland. Birds arriving from Scandinavia enlarge winter gatherings.
species.diet: Invertebrates, especially insect larvae, are important for chicks. Adults also take berries, seeds and grain as food availability changes through the year.
species.behaviour: Walks or runs confidently on the ground and flies directly. Social for much of the year, it may join swirling dusk flocks before roosting.
species.voice: A varied mixture of whistles, clicks, chattering notes and buzzing sounds. Starlings are accomplished mimics.
species.breeding: Builds in cavities in trees or buildings, often nesting near other pairs. Also uses nest boxes.
species.interestingFact: A murmuration's coordinated turns depend on birds responding rapidly to neighbours, allowing a large flock to change shape as it moves through the sky.

species.name: Kingfisher
species.identification: A compact bird with vivid blue upperparts, orange underparts and a long, straight bill. Males have a dark bill; females show orange-pink along the lower half.
species.habitat: Clear, still or gently flowing water, including rivers, canals, lakes and occasionally garden ponds.
species.range: Occurs across much of the UK, with northern Scotland a notable gap. Young birds disperse in search of their own territories after leaving the nest.
species.diet: Catches fish by diving from a waterside perch, sometimes hovering before plunging into the water.
species.behaviour: Often first noticed as a rapid blue flash flying low over the surface. Males vigorously defend valuable feeding areas against rivals.
species.interestingFact: The blue colour comes from microscopic feather structures scattering light rather than blue pigment. A transparent third eyelid also helps the bird keep its prey in sight as it enters the water.

species.name: Kestrel
species.identification: A pointed-winged falcon with a long tail, pale spotted underparts and dark marks beneath the eyes. Males have a grey head and tail; females are browner with several tail bars.
species.habitat: Open grassland, heathland and farmland, including roadside verges. It also hunts suitable open ground within towns and cities.
species.range: Widespread across much of the UK in places where open hunting habitat is available.
species.diet: Voles and other small mammals are important prey, located by watching the ground below.
species.behaviour: Hovers with its tail spread, adjusting wings and tail while keeping its head steady. It may also hunt from a fence post, dropping towards prey once it spots movement.
species.breeding: Uses nesting cavities and suitable nest boxes. A typical clutch contains four or five eggs.
species.interestingFact: The old name windhover reflects its characteristic hunting method. A hovering Kestrel is actively making fine adjustments to hold position, giving it a stable view of the ground beneath.

species.name: Barn Owl
species.identification: A pale owl with a heart-shaped facial disc and dark eyes. Buff and grey mottling covers the back and wings, contrasting with white underparts and conspicuously long legs.
species.habitat: Farmland and rough grassland, where it searches low over the vegetation or watches from a fence post.
species.range: British and Irish birds generally remain resident. The species is absent from much of the far north and west of Scotland, high uplands and urban centres.
species.diet: Small mammals are central to its diet, and their abundance strongly influences how many chicks parents can raise.
species.behaviour: Often seen hunting around dawn or dusk, but may also hunt during daylight, especially in autumn and winter. Its flight is exceptionally quiet.
species.voice: The male gives a prolonged screech early in the breeding season; chicks hiss when begging for food.
species.breeding: Nests in large tree cavities, old farm buildings and nest boxes. Brood size depends strongly on prey availability, with fewer chicks raised in lean years.
species.interestingFact: Most movement by these resident owls occurs when young birds disperse from their birthplace.

species.name: Mallard
species.identification: A substantial duck with a broad bill. In breeding plumage the male has a green head, yellow bill, dark chest and grey body. The female is mottled brown; both sexes show a purple wing patch.
species.habitat: Ponds, lakes and other shallow waters, including some brackish estuaries and coastal lagoons.
species.range: Widespread across suitable UK wetlands, becoming scarcer in high uplands. Many breeding birds remain locally, while winter visitors arrive from Iceland and northern Europe.
species.diet: An adaptable omnivore eating seeds, aquatic plants and small animals, including insect larvae, worms and snails.
species.behaviour: A familiar bird on freshwater ponds. During the rearing season, family groups follow the female across the water.
species.voice: The familiar loud quacking comes from females. Males give softer, rasping calls, while alarmed ducklings whistle.
species.breeding: Nesting can begin as early as February in suitable weather. The female takes responsibility for raising and protecting the ducklings.
species.interestingFact: Ringing records show that winter Mallards visiting Britain and Ireland come from a broad area of Europe, extending east through the Baltic region into Finland and Russia.
